narrative:
The model determined that you have a 76% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is quite high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Placing in the second decile is noticeably lower than the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among students who were accepted. Your first-year class rank was the second most important factor and also worked against you; a third-decile placement falls well below the sixth-decile average of successful applicants. These two academic-standing measures outweighed everything else in the model’s eyes.

Your LSAT score of 38 was the third most influential piece of information, but it worked in the opposite direction. This score sits slightly above the average of accepted students and therefore pulled the prediction modestly toward passing. Unfortunately, the two weaker class-rank signals were simply too powerful for the higher LSAT to overcome.

The model did not consider your gender or race in any way. Family income, undergraduate GPA, and full-time status played only minor roles.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake courses or enroll in a post-baccalaureate program that allows you to demonstrate higher class ranking. Raising your LSAT further could also help, but the data show that consistent high performance in law school coursework carries more weight with this model. Consider reapplying once you can show clearer evidence of strong academic standing.
